reason: Peristome teeth spread or curve outward. The examples describe this correctly.
The examples have no part named. They may describe the stem or the grain, not the spikelet. A rule would need the named part in the text.
Anthers can have setae at the apex or base. The examples are correct.
Some examples say 'spur', which may be a nectar spur and not a short shoot. A rule would need to tell shoot spurs from floral spurs.
'Hooked' and 'falcate' describe hairs, spines or spurs. They are not a short shoot, so this is the wrong part.
Inflorescence branches can be simple (unbranched). The examples fit.
'Exceeding the achene' compares one organ with another, so it is not an absolute length. A rule would need to turn comparisons into a relation or skip them.
Laminae can reflex (bend back). The examples are correct.
Branches can be floccose (tufted woolly hair).
Involucres are often lanate (woolly), as in Asteraceae.
Thorns and spines are hard. The examples fit.
An ovary can be narrow. Some examples refer to the apex, which is slightly off.
Trichomes and hairs can be ascending.
Gemmae are measured as length × width.
This anatomy class can have a diameter. A few examples such as '2–3 × ca. 3 cm' are not diameters.
The examples describe an oblique beak (rostrum) on the operculum, not the operculum's own orientation. A rule would need to attach 'oblique' to the beak.
Leaf colour is meaningful. Some examples are about sheath or stipe, but those are leaf parts.
Stigmas can be dark. 'Dark' fits low brightness.
A staminal column can be hairy.
Apices can be obtuse. 'Rounded' is a near-synonym, so a rule may be needed to separate rounded from obtuse.
Petioles can be weak or stiff.
A cup has a shape (turbinate, goblet-shaped). The examples fit.
Achenes can be keeled. Negated examples ('not keeled') must be handled by the negation rule.
A leaf apex can be retuse (shallowly notched).
'Clathrate' (latticed) describes scales and cell walls, and 'imbriquées' is a different word. The pair comes from a wrong reading, and the part is wrong.
Counting canals is meaningful. Some examples are grooves (sillons), which are a different part.
An involucre margin or lip can be entire, though the quality really belongs to the margin.
PATO 'characteristic' is too generic. The examples are alternatives (ciliate or fimbriate) that need specific terms.
A stem or caudex can be obconical.
A lobe apex can be obtuse.
'Anthers filiform' is fine, but 'filiform trichomes' and 'connective appendages filiform' describe other parts. A rule would need to tell which noun the quality attaches to.
Margins and apices can be revolute (rolled back).
Glands can have colour.
Disc lobes have a length. 'As long as ovary' is a comparison and needs its own handling.
A tuber can have a height.
Stems carry leaf scars.
Filaments can be fusiform (spindle-shaped).
Margins can be crenate (scalloped).
This part can have a height.
'Ovules few' counts the ovules in an ovary. It does not say the ovule has fewer parts, so it is a wrong reading. The part should be the ovary, with a count.
An appendix can be sessile.
Spikelets, or their glumes, can be ciliate.
Sori can be oblique (they are often described this way in ferns).
A disc can be convex.
Veins are spaced a distance apart.
'Shorter than the glume' is a comparison to another organ. A rule would need to handle comparisons separately from absolute length.
Anthers can be woolly or lanulose.
Inflorescence axes and branches have a diameter.
Veins can be oblique.
A banner petal (vexillum) can have a diameter, as the examples show.
Some examples ('short-stalked', 'short-pediceled') describe the stalk, not the spikelet. A rule would need to tell stalk from body.
A corona can be cup-shaped (cupular).
Staminodes can be lobed.
This part can be wide.
A disc can be flattened.
A crown can be flat.
A moss calyptra can be campanulate (bell-shaped).
'Exceeding the capsule' is a comparison, and 'receptacle-tube 35-70 mm long' is a plain length. A rule would need to separate comparisons from lengths.
The examples mix a zigzag, a crest and a mucron, which are different features. The generic 'shape' needs specific terms.
'Sheathlike' (a shape) and 'subsessile' (attachment) are mixed. A rule would need to tell the two apart.
